tests.name: analytic_gradient
tests.title: The implemented gradient equals the analytic policy gradient
tests.what: For a linear softmax policy, compares the gradient PyTorch computes from the surrogate loss with the closed form −Σ_t G_t (e_{a_t} − π(·|s_t)) ⊗ s_t, on single-step bandit episodes with random logits and on multi-step corridor episodes.
tests.how: REINFORCE's update is Σ_t ∇log π(a_t|s_t) G_t and the score of a softmax is e_a − π, so the two must agree to floating-point precision for every action and return; a sign error, a missing return, or a wrong time alignment would show up immediately.

multi-step gradients (returns-to-go, several states) match the closed form to 1e-5

tests.name: bandits
tests.title: Bandits: the policy concentrates on the better arm
tests.what: Trains the policy on one-step problems: a deterministic two-armed bandit with rewards −1 and +1, a Bernoulli bandit with success probabilities 0.3 and 0.7, and a three-armed bandit with positive rewards 0, 1 and 0.5 (10 seeds).
tests.how: Without state or sequence effects, REINFORCE is plain stochastic gradient ascent on E[r], so the probability of the best arm must approach 1 in the first two problems. The third problem documents a known weakness that motivates Part 2: with positive-only rewards and no baseline, every sampled arm is reinforced, so some seeds lock onto the 0.5 arm sampled early; the fraction that still finds the best arm is recorded (and compared with baselines in the Part 2 experiments).

checks.name: deterministic ±1 bandit: P(best arm) > 0.95 after 150 episodes
Bernoulli bandit: P(best arm) > 0.8 after 400 episodes

notes: Positive-only three-armed bandit without baseline: 6/10 seeds found the best arm; the others locked onto the 0.5 arm.

tests.name: corridor_vs_dp
tests.title: REINFORCE reaches the optimum computed by value iteration (corridor)
tests.what: A corridor of 6 cells with the reward at the end (deterministic, and with a 20% chance that a move is reversed). The exact optimal policy and value come from the Section 2 solvers on the same MDP; REINFORCE is trained for 400 episodes and its greedy policy is evaluated exactly on the MDP.
tests.how: Two independent implementations must agree: the greedy policy extracted from the trained network must be 'always right' (the DP optimum), its exact value must equal the DP optimal value, and in the deterministic case the discounted return of a greedy rollout must be γ^(L−2) exactly. The stochastic policy's own average return must be close to the optimum once the per-state probabilities of 'right' are near 1.

tests.name: discount_factor
tests.title: The discount factor decides whether a delayed reward is worth pursuing
tests.what: A 5-cell corridor where every move to the right costs 0.1 and the goal pays 1. For γ ∈ {0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99} the Section 2 solvers give the exact optimal policy of the corresponding MDP (go right from the start or not), and REINFORCE is trained with the same γ (3 seeds, 300 episodes); the success rate at the end of training is compared with what the optimal policy does. Also checks the return weights of one episode.
tests.how: With γ = 0 only the immediate reward counts, so moving right (−0.1) is never worth it and the optimal agent stays at the start; with γ = 0.9 the discounted goal reward outweighs the move costs. Value iteration says exactly which γ flip the decision, and REINFORCE trained with each γ must reproduce that decision: near-zero success where the optimum is to stay, near-certain success where it is to go. This isolates the discount factor from every other part of the algorithm.

tests.name: reward_to_go
tests.title: Three ways to weight the log-probabilities: which agree in expectation
tests.what: With a fixed random policy on a stochastic corridor that charges 0.05 per step (so rewards arrive at every step, not only at the goal), draws 600 single-episode gradient estimates for three weightings of ∇log π(a_t|s_t): the whole-episode return G_0 (classic REINFORCE), γ^t·G_t (the exact gradient of the discounted objective, `--set discount_grad=true`) and the reward-to-go G_t without the γ^t factor (the implementation's default, as in most practical code), and compares means and variances.
tests.how: Rewards earned before step t are independent of a_t given the history, so dropping them does not change the expectation: the G_0 and γ^t·G_t estimates must have the same mean within sampling error, and here the γ^t·G_t weights are pointwise smaller, so its variance must be lower. The default G_t weighting drops the γ^t factor and therefore estimates a slightly different gradient (it treats every visited state as a start state); the experiment records that difference so the choice is a documented one.

checks.name: G_0 and γ^t·G_t have the same mean (within 4 s.e. in every coordinate)
γ^t·G_t has lower total variance than G_0

notes: The default reward-to-go weighting differs from G_0 in expectation (max z = 7.6): it is the usual practical estimator, equal to the exact discounted gradient only when γ = 1.

tests.name: cartpole_short
tests.title: CartPole-v1 learns within 200 episodes on the CPU
tests.what: Trains with the handout's settings (Adam, learning rate 0.01, γ = 0.95) for 300 episodes, seed 0, then evaluates 50 episodes; records the mean reward of the first 20 and of the last 50 training episodes.
tests.how: A correct REINFORCE implementation improves CartPole quickly: the last 50 episodes must average at least 1.5 times the first 20 and at least 100 steps, and the evaluation mean must exceed 50 (random play lasts about 22). The full 1000-episode run and its plots are produced by `python run.py pg --part 1 --env cartpole`.

tests.name: pong_pipeline
tests.title: Pong-v5 pipeline: preprocessing and the two-action restriction
tests.what: Plays one full game of ALE/Pong-v5 with an untrained policy, recording every action sent to the environment and statistics of the preprocessed frame differences the network sees.
tests.how: The handout restricts the agent to RIGHT (2) and LEFT (3): every recorded action must be one of them. The preprocessed input must be an 80×80 image with values in {−1, 0, 1} (frame difference of binary frames) that is non-zero most of the time (the ball and paddles move), and a game must end with a score between −21 and 21 (an untrained agent loses almost every point).
